title: Rome and Carthage
hook: A struggle for Sicily became a contest across the western Mediterranean.
notes: Historical locations are approximate city/site anchors, not surveyed battle sites or territorial polygons. No modern state is used as a proxy for Roman sovereignty. Events follow cited ancient accounts and institutional histories; ancient authors are not neutral eyewitnesses to every event. BC dates use astronomical years internally. Polybius Histories 1, 3 and 15; Appian Punic Wars 127–135. These ancient narratives supply chronology. Zama and the Alpine crossing remain geographically uncertain.

scenes.title: Across the water
scenes.text: Italy and the African coast faced each other across Sicily. Polybius traces the first war to intervention on that island in 264 BC.

scenes.title: The war moves north
scenes.text: Hannibal carried the next war from Iberia across the Alps into Italy in 218 BC. The map anchors his arrival in the Po valley and his victory at Cannae; it does not invent his disputed route.

scenes.title: The decision in Africa
scenes.text: At Zama in 202 BC, Scipio defeated Hannibal. Victory shifted the balance toward Rome, but Carthage survived the peace.

scenes.title: A city destroyed
scenes.text: In 146 BC another Roman army destroyed Carthage. Compare the African battle-region marker with the coastal city: conquest involved both armies in the field and the destruction of urban communities.
